Buying a home, without the guesswork

Buying in Scottsdale, Paradise Valley, or Fountain Hills means paying desert prices. The job is to make sure the home is worth it. Here is how I work with buyers, step by step.

1

A short first conversation

We talk through what you need, where you want to be, and what you can comfortably spend. If you need a lender, I will point you to ones who close on time in this market.

2

A search built around you

You get MLS listings that match your criteria as they come up, not a drip of homes that almost fit. We tour the strong candidates and skip the rest.

3

An honest price check on every home

Before you offer, I show you the comparable sales and tell you plainly whether the asking price is fair, high, or low, and why.

4

An offer written to win, carefully

Price matters, but so do terms: timelines, contingencies, and how clean the offer looks to a seller. My years on the builder side taught me exactly how sellers read offers.

5

Inspections, appraisal, and closing

I coordinate the inspection, review the results with you in plain language, and keep the lender, title company, and seller on schedule through closing day.

Selling for what your home is really worth

Price too high and your home sits while buyers move on. Price too low and you give money away. Good selling is mostly good pricing, honest preparation, and strong presentation, in that order.

Pricing from evidence

I price from recent closed sales of homes like yours, adjusted for condition, lot, and view, and I show you every comparable I used. You will understand the number before we agree on it.

Preparation that pays

Most homes do not need a remodel before selling. They need the right repairs, a short list of high return fixes, and a clean, uncluttered presentation. I will tell you exactly what is worth doing and what is not.

Presentation and marketing

Professional photography, a listing description written around how people will actually live in the home, and placement in front of the buyer pool most likely to pay for it, including my network of agents and builder contacts.

Negotiation and closing

When offers come in, I lay out each one clearly: price, terms, financing strength, and risk. Then I negotiate from the strength of the evidence we built at pricing time.

What sellers usually ask me

  • When is the best time to list? Late winter through spring brings the most buyers to the desert, but a well priced home sells in any month. Your timeline matters more than the calendar.
  • Should I fix things first? Safety and obvious defects, yes. Big remodels, almost never. Ask me before you spend anything.
  • What will selling cost? I will give you a written estimate of every cost, including commissions, title, and closing fees, before you sign anything.

Luxury homes, handled quietly and well

An estate in Paradise Valley or a custom home in north Scottsdale is not sold the way a starter home is sold. The buyer pool is smaller, the expectations are higher, and discretion matters.

What luxury selling actually takes

  • Preparation without waste. The right staging, lighting, and repair list for a home where every detail gets judged.
  • Photography and film that respect the home. Shot at the right hour, in the right light, showing scale and setting honestly.
  • The right audience. Qualified buyers and the agents who represent them, including out of state buyers relocating to the desert.
  • Privacy. Showings by appointment, qualified visitors only, and your plans kept off the public record for as long as possible.
  • A steady negotiator. Large numbers invite large emotions. My job is to keep the conversation on evidence and terms.

Buying a luxury home?

Some of the finest homes here are sold quietly, through agent networks rather than public listings. Tell me what you are looking for and I will work those channels as well as the open market. I will also give you a straight assessment of value. In Paradise Valley, where the median price sits around $4.2 million, two homes on the same street can differ by a million dollars for reasons that are not obvious from photos.

My background fits this end of the market

I worked with high end buyers and builder partners across the country. Combined with eleven years at Shea Homes, that gives me relationships with the builders, architects, and agents who shape this market.

Buying new construction, from someone who sold it

From 2012 to 2023 I worked inside Shea Homes, in sales, community management, and sales leadership. I have sat in the sales office chair, run lot releases, and priced options. Here is how new construction buying actually works, and where having your own agent protects you.

How a builder sales office really works

The people in the model home office are good at their jobs, and their job is to sell homes for the builder at the builder's price. They are not your agent, and they are not neutral. They work from a release schedule: a set number of lots at a time, priced against the last release, often with quiet increases built in as the community sells. When a sales associate says a price is going up next month, that is usually true, because the release calendar says so.

Good communities often keep interest lists before lots are released. Where you sit on that list, and how prepared you are with financing, can decide whether you get the lot you want. I know how those lists are worked because I worked them.

Bring your own agent. The builder expects it.

Builders plan for buyers to have agents. In most cases the builder pays the buyer's agent, and the price of the home does not drop if you show up without one. The savings stay with the builder. What you give up by going alone is representation: someone to review the contract, watch the build, and negotiate where negotiation is possible.

One rule matters more than any other: your agent must be registered on your first visit. If you walk into a sales office or register online without naming your agent, many builders will not recognize your representation afterward. Call me before you visit a model home, even just to look. It takes two minutes and it protects your options.

Lot premiums: paying for position

The base price buys the least desirable lot in the release. Corner lots, larger lots, lots backing to open space or mountains, and lots on quiet interior streets carry premiums that can run from a few thousand dollars to well over one hundred thousand on larger homesites. Some premiums hold their value at resale, especially view and open space lots. Some do not. A premium for a lot next to a future phase of construction, for example, buys you years of noise. I will tell you which ones I would pay and which I would not.

The design center: where the margin lives

Builders make a modest margin on the base home and a strong one on options. Flooring, cabinets, countertops, lighting, and built-ins at the design center are priced well above what the same work costs after closing with your own contractors. That does not make every option a bad buy. Structural choices, ceiling heights, added rooms, extended patios, ceiling fan and outlet placements, and anything inside the walls are worth doing during the build, because they are expensive or impossible later. Cosmetic finishes you can do after closing for less. Part of my job is sitting with your option list and sorting one from the other before you sign.

Builder contracts are not the standard contract

Arizona has a standard purchase contract that most resale homes use. Builders use their own contracts, written by their own lawyers. Expect differences that matter: deposits that are harder to recover, tight deadlines for design choices, financing terms that favor the builder's lender, limited rights if the builder is delayed, and arbitration clauses. None of this is a reason to walk away. It is a reason to read carefully, with someone who has read hundreds of them, before you sign.

Yes, a brand new home needs inspections

Cities inspect new builds at stages, but those inspections check code minimums and move fast. They are not done for you. I recommend two independent inspections: one before the drywall goes up, when framing, plumbing, and wiring are still visible, if the builder's schedule allows it, and one before closing, covering everything from roof tiles to drainage. New homes have defects. The point of inspecting is finding them while the builder is still responsible for fixing them.

Timelines, incentives, and rate buydowns

Builders quote build times that assume everything goes right. Weather is rarely the problem here; labor, materials, and permit queues are. Plan for delays, and do not schedule your life, a lease ending or a sale closing, tight against a promised completion date. On incentives: builders prefer offering money toward closing costs, design options, or an interest rate buydown through their lender rather than cutting the base price, because the base price sets the value of the next release. A buydown can be genuinely valuable. So can cash. I will run both side by side so you can see which one leaves you better off.

The walkthrough: slow down, look closely

Before closing you walk the home with the builder's representative and list anything unfinished or wrong. This is not a celebration tour. I attend walkthroughs with my buyers and I bring a checklist: every outlet and switch, every faucet and drain, doors and windows, paint and drywall under angled light, appliances run through a cycle, irrigation and drainage outside, and the slope of the yard away from the house. Anything promised gets written on the walkthrough list, because what is written gets fixed and what is said often does not.

Investment property, judged by the numbers

A rental home in the Phoenix area can be a sound long term holding. It can also be a slow leak. The difference is in the arithmetic before you buy, and I will do that arithmetic with you honestly.

Rent you can count on

We estimate rent from actual leased comparables nearby, not the optimistic figure in a listing description.

Every cost on the table

Taxes, insurance, HOA fees, maintenance, vacancy, and management, whether you plan to manage the home yourself or hire it out.

An exit you understand

Who buys this home from you later, and why? Appreciation in the right Scottsdale and Fountain Hills neighborhoods has historically rewarded patient owners, but we buy for the cash flow first.

How I evaluate a property with you

We start with the likely monthly rent, subtract a realistic allowance for vacancy and repairs, then subtract taxes, insurance, HOA dues, and management. What is left, compared with the cash you put in, is the return that matters. If the numbers do not work at the asking price, I will say so and tell you the price at which they would.

I also flag the things spreadsheets miss: an HOA that restricts rentals, a roof near the end of its life, a floor plan that rents poorly, or a street that is improving fast enough to change the math. My years pricing new homes for a builder taught me to spot all four quickly.

Second homes and seasonal rentals

Many of my clients buy a desert home they use part of the year and rent the rest. The rules differ by city and by HOA, and they change. I will walk you through what is allowed where you are buying before you count on any rental income.

Market analysis you can actually use

Good decisions need good information. I work from real transaction data out of ARMLS, the regional multiple listing service, and I will show you the numbers behind any advice I give.

Pricing a home to sell

Price too high and the home sits, often selling for less in the end. Price too low and you leave money behind. A careful comparable analysis protects you from both.

Judging an asking price

Before you offer, know whether the price is fair. Understanding a home's market position tells you how firmly you need to negotiate.

Spotting a fair opportunity

Accurate data separates a sound purchase from an expensive mistake, and it shows you where a seller may be ready to move on price or terms.

What I look at

  • Closed sales, not asking prices. What homes actually sold for is the ground truth. List prices are wishes.
  • Days on market. This market has clear seasonal patterns. How long homes like yours take to sell shapes both pricing and strategy.
  • Supply in your price band. A shortage of competing homes gives a seller strength. A crowded field gives a buyer choices.
  • Price reductions. A pattern of cuts in a neighborhood is information you want before you list or offer.

Whether you need a valuation for your own home, an analysis of a neighborhood you are considering, or a clear eyed look at an investment, I will prepare it from the same data I would use for my own money.

Scottsdale

Scottsdale runs about thirty miles from south to north, and the two ends feel like different cities. Knowing which Scottsdale fits your life is the first real decision.

South Scottsdale and Old Town put you near restaurants, spring training baseball, galleries, and the valley's best nightlife. Homes here range from mid century ranches and condos to new townhomes. It suits buyers who want to walk to dinner and be twenty minutes from the airport.

Central Scottsdale, around McCormick Ranch and Gainey Ranch, is established and green, with lakes, golf, and larger lots from the 1970s and 1980s, much of it now remodeled. Families like the balance of space, schools, and location.

North Scottsdale is newer, quieter, and more expensive: master planned communities like Grayhawk, DC Ranch, and Silverleaf, desert landscaping, mountain views, and some of the finest custom homes in the state. This is also where new construction is most active, which is where my builder background earns its keep.

Buying in Scottsdale

Prices vary enormously by neighborhood and even by street, so comparable sales matter more here than almost anywhere in Arizona. HOA fees vary just as much. Part of my job is showing you the full cost picture of each community, not just the list price.

Search Scottsdale homes

Paradise Valley

A town of roughly 12,000 people between Camelback Mountain and the McDowell Mountains, built around one idea: homes, and only homes, on generous lots.

Paradise Valley has almost no commercial development. What it has instead are acre lots, mature desert landscaping, quiet streets, and views in every direction. The median sale price sits around $4.2 million, and the town's resorts, including Camelback Inn and Sanctuary, sit tucked into the mountain foothills at its edges.

Most homes here are custom, and many are substantial: estates with guest houses, resort level backyards, and architecture ranging from classic ranch to striking contemporary. Because no two homes are alike, pricing one, buying or selling, depends on deep local knowledge rather than simple square foot math.

Buying or selling here

Privacy is part of the product. Many sales happen with little public notice, and showings are handled carefully. If you are buying, I will give you a straight read on value lot by lot, since position, view corridor, and mountain proximity move prices by seven figures. If you are selling, preparation and the right buyer audience matter more than broad exposure.

Search Paradise Valley homes

Fountain Hills

My home town since 2018. A community of about 23,000 people in the McDowell Mountain foothills, about thirty minutes northeast of Scottsdale, and a genuinely different pace of life.

The town grew up around its fountain, which sends water 330 feet into the air at the center of Fountain Park. Around it you will find a friendly, unhurried town: local restaurants, an active arts scene, dark skies, and trailheads that start where neighborhoods end. The Four Peaks and the McDowells frame nearly every view.

Homes range from lock and leave townhomes and single story houses that suit winter residents, up to custom homes on hillside lots with long views toward the valley lights. Compared with Scottsdale and Paradise Valley, your money goes noticeably further here, and many buyers find the trade, a short drive for a quieter life, easy to make.

Why I recommend it, honestly

I chose to live and raise my family here, which is the strongest endorsement I can give any town. It is not for everyone. If you want walkable nightlife, Scottsdale fits better. If you want space, views, quiet, and a town where people know each other, Fountain Hills is hard to beat.

Who is Mike Coffey?

Mike Coffey (Michael Patrick Coffey) is a REALTOR in Arizona, licensed under number SA653573000, working with the brokerage LPT Realty. He specializes in luxury residential real estate in Scottsdale, Paradise Valley, and Fountain Hills.

What is his background in new construction?

How do commissions work when buying?

Commission terms are agreed in writing before you buy. In many transactions the seller offers compensation that covers the buyer's agent, but the exact arrangement depends on the home and the agreement you sign. Mike Coffey explains the full cost picture in writing before you make an offer, so there are no surprises at closing.

What does a home valuation include?

A home valuation from Mike Coffey is a personal analysis based on recent closed sales of similar homes near yours, adjusted for size, condition, lot, and view. It includes a realistic price range and the reasoning behind it. It is prepared by Mike personally, not generated by an automated estimate tool. You can request one on the home value page.

Should I bring my own agent when buying a new construction home?

Yes. The builder's sales staff work for the builder, not for you. Having your own agent costs you nothing extra in most cases, because the builder typically pays the buyer's agent. Register your agent on your first visit to the sales office, or the builder may refuse to recognize your representation later. Mike Coffey spent 2012 to 2023 at Shea Homes and knows builder sales from the inside. More on the new construction page.

Does a new construction home still need an inspection?

Yes. City inspections check code minimums during construction, but they are not a substitute for your own independent inspection. Mike Coffey recommends an independent inspection before the walls are closed in, when possible, and again before closing, in addition to attending the builder walkthrough.
